clue.text: Clubs prompt with booze

parts.note: C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs
to prompt a feeling is to arouse or stir it up

explanation.surface: Someone urges a group of nightclubs to serve alcohol, or prods a friend into drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'booze' is a verb here: to drink heavily and merrily.
explanation.definitionFit: To carouse is to drink plentifully in a noisy, sociable revel.

clue.text: It's hecate wrongly associated with beauty

indicators.note: written wrongly, the letters of these two words are jumbled into a different order

parts.note: the contraction of 'it is' supplies its three letters I, T, S

explanation.surface: Someone protests that the witch-goddess Hecate has been wrongly linked with beauty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrongly' shuffles the nine letters of IT'S HECATE; the apostrophe adds no letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesthetic describes anything concerned with the appreciation of beauty and art.

clue.text: Former mistresses separated in French city

definitions.meaning: an archaic word for lovers or sweethearts, plural
the town in the Sarthe famous for its 24-hour motor race

explanation.surface: Ex-lovers have split up and now live apart in a French town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'separated' tells you the city's name is written as two words, LE MANS, while the archaic plural for paramours runs them together.
explanation.definitionFit: Leman is an old word for a sweetheart or illicit lover; Le Mans is a city in north-west France.

clue.text: Strict lawyer on a roll

parts.note: in cricket the on side is also called the leg side, so on gives leg
a roll is a register or list of names

explanation.surface: A rigid attorney is enjoying a winning streak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on a roll' looks like an idiom for a lucky run; it splits into ON (cricket's leg side), A and ROLL (a list). In cricket the half of the field behind the batter's legs is called both the on side and the leg side.
explanation.definitionFit: A legalist insists on strict, literal adherence to law and rules.

clue.text: Order direct and you get these guarantees

parts.note: putting the six letters of the word direct into a new order yields the word credit

explanation.surface: Place your order straight with the supplier and you will receive the bank's assurances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order direct' looks like advice to buy without a middleman; read it as 'rearrange DIRECT'. That gives CREDIT, so these are the letters of 'credit', a punning name for bank guarantees.
explanation.definitionFit: A letter of credit is a bank's written undertaking that a buyer's payment will be made, a financial guarantee.

clue.text: Virginia's partner into endless marijuana? That's serious

definitions.note: the clue's adjective stands for the noun meaning a serious, weighty manner

indicators.note: the partner's name goes into the shortened slang word for the drug
the slang word loses its final letter, so it has no end

parts.note: grass is slang for marijuana
Vita Sackville-West was the lover of the novelist Virginia Woolf

explanation.surface: A joke that someone's companion has got stoned, followed by a sober remark that it is no laughing matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Virginia' looks like the US state but is Virginia Woolf, whose lover was Vita Sackville-West. 'That's serious' frames the definition as a comment on the surface joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Gravitas is dignity and weightiness of manner, the quality of being serious.

clue.text: Girl showing how to get dla

parts.note: these three letters are made by placing the letter l inside the pair d, a

explanation.surface: A girl demonstrating how to obtain a mysterious thing called dla.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the name as an instruction, L IN DA: put L inside DA and you get DLA.
explanation.definitionFit: Linda is a common female first name.

clue.text: No parking in st Peter's, try these outside

indicators.note: try is read as an instruction to have a go at arranging the remaining letters another way
the word no means the parking sign's letter is left out of the saint's name

parts.note: P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking

explanation.surface: A notice says parking is banned at St Peter's church, so try the roads round about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No ... in' takes the P out of ST PETER'S, leaving STETERS, and 'try' rearranges those letters. The definition points to the roads outside the church.
explanation.definitionFit: Streets are the public roads out of doors where a driver might look for a space instead.

clue.text: Some Milanese rave about an Italian city

indicators.note: about means the run of letters is turned round to read the other way
only some of the letters of these two words are used, a run within them

explanation.surface: A few people from Milan enthuse wildly about one of their country's cities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' picks ESERAV from inside MILANESE RAVE, and 'about' turns that run round.
explanation.definitionFit: Varese is a city in Lombardy, north-west of Milan.

clue.text: The queen boards coaches — not in these!

indicators.note: to board is to get on, so the monarch's letters go inside the coaches

parts.note: railway coaches coupled together make trains
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword abbreviation for the queen

explanation.surface: The monarch climbs aboard a railway carriage, though apparently not in sports shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coaches' looks like the definition (trainers are coaches) but is the wordplay. The definition is a dress-code warning: smart clubs often refuse entry to people in sports shoes.
explanation.definitionFit: Trainers are casual sports shoes, the footwear many smart venues and dress codes ban.

clue.text: Shorten Tory pamphlet

parts.note: Con is the short form for Conservative, the party of the Tories
a tract is a short pamphlet, often religious or political

explanation.surface: A command to cut down a Conservative party leaflet.
explanation.walkthrough: CON is the standard abbreviation for Conservative, the UK party whose members are called Tories.
explanation.definitionFit: To contract is to draw together and become or make smaller.

clue.text: Recall note covering for example, white horse inn?

indicators.note: the turned note goes round the outside of the horse
recall is read as calling back, so the musical note is turned to read backwards

parts.note: ti is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale, also written te
a mare is a female horse, and a white one would be an example

explanation.surface: Remembering a note left at a pub called the White Horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recall' turns the note round, and 'covering' wraps it round the horse. 'White horse inn' looks like a pub name, but 'inn?' alone is the definition; the question mark flags an unusual example of an inn.
explanation.definitionFit: An imaret is a Turkish hospice where travellers and pilgrims are lodged, a kind of hostelry.

clue.text: Berks so right to get a property valuer

parts.note: berk is British slang for a fool, so berks are asses
taken as written

explanation.surface: Fools, apparently, are just the people to value your house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Berks' looks like the English county Berkshire, but it is the British slang for idiots.
explanation.definitionFit: An assessor values property, for instance to fix its rateable value for tax.

clue.text: Haar around west of England is extremely unpleasant

indicators.note: the fog's letters go around the single letter taken from England

parts.note: haar is a cold sea mist or fog on the east coast of Scotland and England

indicators.note: in a horizontal word the west is the left side, so this takes the opening letter

explanation.surface: A grumble that the sea fog over western England is truly miserable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'west of' gives E, the first letter of England, and 'around' puts SEA MIST round it. Haar is a dialect word from eastern Scotland and north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Seamiest is the superlative of seamy, meaning sordid and disreputable.

clue.text: Home kind? The opposite

parts.note: to be in is to be at home
a version is a particular kind or variant of something

explanation.surface: Asked what sort of home is wanted, someone answers with the reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home' looks like a noun, but here it means 'at home', which is IN.
explanation.definitionFit: An inversion is a reversal of order or position, turning something into its contrary.

clue.text: Mark catches the rector out

indicators.note: the mark holds the other letters within itself, as if catching them

parts.note: to note something is to mark it

explanation.surface: Someone called Mark finds the parish priest away from home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' looks like a man's name but is a verb meaning to jot down; 'catches' holds the next words inside it. The definition 'out' means not at home.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is out is absent, away from the place where they would be.

clue.text: Heard Russian dramatist? Tick list

indicators.note: heard tells you the dramatist's name is said out loud and a phrase that sounds alike is entered

parts.note: Anton Chekhov wrote The Seagull and The Cherry Orchard

explanation.surface: Someone hears of a Russian playwright and ticks him off a reading list.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tick list' is a verb and its object: to tick items on a list.
explanation.definitionFit: To check off items is to mark them with a tick as each is dealt with.

clue.text: Ecstasy used in own house leads to dismissal

indicators.note: the drug's letter is placed inside the verb meaning possess

parts.note: to own something is to have it
E is the street name for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: Drug-taking in someone's own home gets them thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leads to' is the link to the definition. 'used in' puts the drug's letter inside the verb before the house abbreviation follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving someone the heave-ho means sacking or rejecting them unceremoniously.

clue.text: Did recount and Republican's over the moon

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for Republican; the 's stands for 'is' and adds no letter
over the moon is an idiom for delighted

explanation.surface: After an election recount, the Republican is overjoyed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recount' looks like an election recount, but it means narrate.
explanation.definitionFit: Related, as a past-tense verb, means told or narrated a story.

clue.text: Provide food and drink around the tube

indicators.note: the caterer's verb goes around the word the

parts.note: to cater is to supply food and drink, for example at a function

explanation.surface: An instruction to serve refreshments around the Underground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tube' looks like London's Underground, but it is a medical tube.
explanation.definitionFit: A catheter is a thin flexible tube inserted into the body, typically to drain the bladder.

clue.text: Carmen seen in the ancient Balkan country

indicators.note: the motoring club's letters are seen inside the word the

parts.note: read as car men, the motorists of the RAC, the Royal Automobile Club

explanation.surface: The opera heroine Carmen spotted in an old land of the Balkans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carmen' looks like Bizet's heroine; split it as 'car men', the RAC, Britain's Royal Automobile Club motoring organisation.
explanation.definitionFit: Thrace was an ancient region of south-east Europe, now split between Greece, Bulgaria and Turkey.

clue.text: Curse Chinese dipstick

parts.note: the Han are the main ethnic group of China
dipstick and git are both British slang for a stupid person

explanation.surface: Someone swears at a foolish Chinese man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dipstick' looks like the oil gauge in a car; it is slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Hang it! is a mild exclamation of annoyance, a minced oath.

clue.text: Old batsman observed before lunch?

definitions.meaning: a short prayer said before a meal

explanation.walkthrough: W.G. Grace was England's most famous nineteenth-century cricketer. 'Observed' means kept as a custom, as a prayer is.
explanation.definitionFit: Grace was a legendary cricketer; grace is also the prayer of thanks said before eating.

clue.text: Tours are arranged by this service

indicators.note: these two words are arranged differently, their letters set in a new order

explanation.surface: Holiday tours are organised by a particular company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arranged' rearranges the eight letters of TOURS ARE. Eurostar runs trains through the Channel Tunnel.
explanation.definitionFit: Eurostar is the high-speed rail link between London and continental Europe.

clue.text: Fancy aged banks detest backing advance

indicators.note: the jumbled letters bank, or line both sides of, the turned word
fancy as an adjective means elaborate, so these letters are rearranged
backing means the word for loathe is read backwards

parts.note: to detest is to hate

explanation.surface: Elderly people who loathe banks backing a loan sounds like a financial story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' turns AGED into GEAD, 'backing' turns HATE into ETAH, and 'banks' puts G-EAD either side of it.
explanation.definitionFit: To get ahead is to make progress and succeed, especially in a career.

clue.text: Old head of English in school called to attract attention

indicators.note: the two letters go inside the word for the school

parts.note: a coed is a coeducational school, for boys and girls

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: An old English head teacher shouted to get pupils to listen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head of English' looks like a teacher; it gives only E. 'in' puts O and E inside COED.
explanation.definitionFit: Cooee is the Australian hailing cry, so to have cooeed is to have shouted to get notice.

clue.text: Most recent work upfront lost irrevocably

indicators.note: the word for work comes up front, before the other piece

parts.note: a machine that goes is working
the most recent thing is the newest

explanation.surface: The latest work at the front is gone for good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'work' is a verb here: GO, as in 'the clock goes'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gone west is an idiom for lost, dead or destroyed past recovery.
